name: Maximum drawdown
brief:
Maximum drawdown is the worst fall from a high to a later low. Risk reports quote it beside volatility. It is the loss you would have sat through if you bought at the top.

Write `max_drawdown(prices)`. It takes prices in time order and returns the maximum drawdown as a fraction from 0 to 1.
definition:
The drawdown on day $t$ compares the price with the highest price so far:

$$D_t = 1 - \dfrac{P_t}{\max\limits_{s \le t} P_s}$$

The maximum drawdown is $\max_t D_t$. Return `0.0` for an empty list or a single price. Every price is a positive float.
constraints: $O(n)$ time, where $n$ is the number of prices. One pass is enough.
Standard library only. NumPy and pandas are not loaded.
All tests share a 5-second time limit.
hint: Walk the list once and carry two numbers: the highest price so far, and the largest drawdown so far. Each new price either raises the peak or is measured against it.
starter:
def max_drawdown(prices):
    """Return the maximum drawdown
    of prices, as a fraction."""
    # Your code here
    return 0.0

examples.note: The peak is 120 and the lowest later price is 90, so $1 - \tfrac{90}{120} = 0.25$.
The fall from 50 to 40 is 0.2. Then the new high of 60 falls to 30, which is $1 - \tfrac{30}{60} = 0.5$.
The fall from 100 to 90 is 0.1. The rise to 95 does not change it.

tests.name: Empty list
tests.why: With no prices there is nothing to fall from. Return `0.0` before you read `prices[0]`.

tests.name: Single price
tests.why: One price has no later low, so its drawdown is `0.0`.

tests.name: Rising prices
tests.why: Prices that only rise never fall from a high. Measure each price against the highest price so far, not the overall high.

tests.name: Falling prices
tests.why: The first price is the peak and every later price sits below it. Make sure the first day counts.

tests.name: Crash, then recovery
tests.why: A recovery does not undo the loss. Keep the largest drawdown, not the latest one.

tests.name: New high after a drawdown
tests.why: After 120 the peak is 120, not 100. Move the peak up whenever the price makes a new high.

tests.name: Smaller second drawdown
tests.why: The second fall, 110 to 99, is smaller than the first. Keep the largest drawdown seen so far.

tests.name: Daily closes
tests.why: Return a fraction of the peak, $1 - P_t / \text{peak}$, not a percentage or a price gap. Do not round.

tests.name: Fall on the last day
tests.why: The worst fall comes on the final price. Check that your loop reaches the last element.

tests.name: Long series
tests.note: 200,000 prices from a seeded random walk
tests.why: This test has 200,000 prices. A loop inside a loop takes about $2 \times 10^{10}$ steps here; one pass takes $2 \times 10^{5}$.

how: Submit runs 10 hidden tests, from an empty list to 200,000 prices. A float counts when it is within a relative 1e-9 of the expected value, so `0.30000000000000004` counts as `0.3`.
where: Part of the 1.1 exit project: returns, annualised volatility and maximum drawdown from a CSV of daily prices.
solution:
def max_drawdown(prices):
    # Highest price so far
    peak = 0.0
    # Largest drawdown so far
    worst = 0.0
    for p in prices:
        peak = max(peak, p)
        worst = max(worst, 1 - p / peak)
    return worst
notes: `peak` holds the highest price so far, so each price is measured against the right high.
`worst` keeps the largest drawdown, so a later recovery cannot erase it.
Each price is read once: $O(n)$ time and $O(1)$ extra memory. Starting `peak` at `0.0` is safe because every price is positive.
prelude:
def _walk(n, seed, start, step):
    # Seeded random walk from an integer LCG, so every Python makes the same prices
    x = seed
    p = start
    out = []
    for _ in range(n):
        x = (x * 1103515245 + 12345) % 2147483648
        p = p * (1 + step * ((x % 2001 - 1000) / 1000))
        out.append(p)
    return out
